source.title: iShumei-Chinchunmei at SemEval-2025 Task 4: A balanced forgetting and retention multi-task framework using effective unlearning loss

record.tranche_reason: The paper develops and evaluates its own unlearning method using benchmark forgetting, task, and capability metrics. It does not test whether attacks recover knowledge after unlearning, which is the focus of the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The study reports unlearning benchmark results for EUL, including MIA and task scores, but does not test fine-tuning recovery, activation ablation, quantization, or prompt-based recovery. Its MIA metric is described as an evaluation metric, not as an attack applied after unlearning. It also gives no comparison with a model that never saw the targeted knowledge.
record.test_reason: This SemEval-2025 Task 4 system paper proposes EUL, an inverse-NTP loss with retain-set SFT, and reports only its own benchmark scores (TAS, MIA, MMLU) on OLMo-1B/7B. It applies no post-unlearning recovery attack: no relearning, ablation, quantization or prompting. It gives no robustness claim against such attacks. It cites Eldan & Russinovich only as background. So none of the versions A–F is tested; the paper is the method's own performance report.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that EUL with retain-set SFT in a multi-task framework gives controllable unlearning while preserving general capability. They find that retain-set SFT is essential and that re-segmentation data augmentation helps. They also note that the submitted leaderboard entry (RD&NR&EUL, 5th place) was not their best configuration (RD&DA&EUL). They draw no conclusions about recovery attacks.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes EUL, an inverse next-token-prediction loss, in a multi-task training setup; it does not reproduce the original methods or test the recovery attacks in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported benchmark outcomes vary with data augmentation, training steps, epoch, and learning rate.

fits_no_version.finding: On OLMo-1B, EUL+RD+DA gives MIA 0.593, TAS 0.395, MMLU 0.275. Matched-step training without DA gives 0.175 / 0.306 / 0.286. Configurations without retain-set SFT reach higher MIA/TAS but MMLU drops to 0.229.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benchmark forgetting/retention trade-offs of an inverse-loss unlearning method depend on retain-set SFT, data augmentation, epochs and learning rate. This says nothing about recoverability.

record.problems: No post-unlearning recovery attacks or never-trained comparison are reported. The relevant benchmark scores do not directly measure recovery; no uncertainty estimates are stated.
record.rows_left_out: Additional EUL configurations and hyperparameter results in Tables 1–6 and Appendix A were not extracted because they report benchmark performance of the proposed method, not outcomes of the recovery attacks in the claim.

untested.parts: Whether simple attacks recover forgotten content. Near-chance targeted accuracy relative to a reference model is not reported either.
Relearning by fine-tuning on unrelated, related or forget-subset data.
Activation-direction ablation, or analysis of blocking versus deletion.
Rephrasing, jailbreak, multilingual or in-context recovery.
No claim or test of resistance to recovery attacks.

record.verdict_notes: The relation was changed from 'discusses' to 'cites_only'. The paper does not discuss shallow unlearning or recovery; it only cites WHP among prior methods. MIA is the organizers' evaluation metric, not an attack run on the unlearned model. The OLMo-7B results in the appendix are declared in rows_left_out and also bear on no version.

versions.untested_parts: Whether a simple attack recovers targeted knowledge after unlearning; the study does not report near-chance targeted accuracy in a way that tests this version.
Recovery by fine-tuning on unrelated, loosely related, or forgotten examples.
Recovery by ablating an activation direction or evidence that unlearning blocks access rather than deleting knowledge.
Recovery through rephrasing, jailbreaks, other languages, or in-context information.
Resistance to the attacks listed in the claim.

relation.reason: It cites Eldan & Russinovich 2023 (an original) only in Background, to describe its method. It never discusses whether unlearning is recoverable.

tranche.reason: Proposes its own unlearning loss (EUL) and reports only SemEval benchmark scores (TAS, MIA, MMLU). It runs no relearning, ablation, quantization or prompting attack, so it neither tests nor uses the shallow-unlearning finding.

source_check.notes: The rows match Tables 1 to 3. Table 1 is garbled in the text, but RD&DA&EUL values are confirmed in Tables 2, 3 and 5. r4/r6/r8 duplicate r1 to r3. The no-DA comparators (r5/r7/r9) are step-matched at 807 steps, which is 11.45 epochs, not 5. The MIA scale is undefined, OLMo-1B MMLU (0.23 to 0.29) is near chance, and no pre-unlearning reference is given. No verdicts.
